analysis.one_liner: Lets money market funds go back to fixed $1 share pricing while barring direct federal bailouts of the funds.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote and died in the Senate Banking Committee when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2008 financial crisis, regulators required large institutional money market funds to let their share prices float and to charge fees that discourage investors from fleeing at the first sign of trouble. This bill would let any money market fund promise a fixed $1 share price again, and exempt funds making that choice from the default liquidity fee. It also prohibits direct federal bailouts of money market funds and requires funds to disclose that ban to investors — but the ban does not cover broad-based Federal Reserve emergency programs, the type actually used to support the industry in 2008 and 2020.
analysis.who_benefits: Money market fund companies regain the ability to offer fixed-$1 share pricing to all investors, including large institutional ones, without the default liquidity fees, making those funds easier to market and cheaper to run. Institutional and corporate cash investors get back the stable-priced product they preferred before the reforms.

how_it_helps.text: Any money market fund could elect to price shares using the amortized cost or penny-rounding method — a stable $1 price — regardless of whether its shareholders are natural persons or institutions.
Funds making that election would be exempt from the default liquidity fee requirement that regulators imposed after the crisis.

The bill bans direct federal assistance — loans, stock purchases, guarantees, loss-sharing, or related tax breaks — to any money market fund, and requires that prohibition to be prominently disclosed in fund prospectuses, advertising, and sales materials.

analysis.who_pays: If a stable-priced fund got into trouble, the fixed $1 price would recreate the incentive for investors to run out the door first, the dynamic behind the 2008 crisis. The risk of market disruption, and of support arriving through broad-based emergency programs not covered by the bill's ban, would fall on taxpayers and on ordinary investors in the broader financial system.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and the broader financial system

drawbacks.text: A fixed $1 share price is what created the run risk in 2008: because investors know the price cannot fall, they race to redeem at the first hint of trouble, forcing funds to sell assets into a falling market. The floating-price requirement and liquidity fees adopted after the crisis were designed to reduce that dynamic, and this bill would waive both for electing funds.

The bailout prohibition covers only direct assistance to a fund. It expressly excludes Federal Reserve facilities with broad-based eligibility established in unusual or exigent circumstances — the very mechanism used to backstop the money market industry in 2008 and again in March 2020 — so the most likely route for future support would remain open.
Even supporters of investor choice would have to acknowledge that removing the default liquidity fee removes a buffer meant to make redeeming during stress more expensive and slow the run.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Investors who want a stable-priced fund gain a genuine choice, and the disclosure requirement is honest labeling. But the costs are real: the stable-price promise is the mechanism that produced the 2008 money market runs, and the bailout ban's carve-out for broad-based emergency programs means the industry could still be rescued indirectly. The bill trades a post-crisis safeguard for industry flexibility while advertising a no-bailout pledge it does not fully deliver.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Toomey introduced the bill on March 11, 2019, joined by Senators Menendez, Rounds, and Peters, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
The complete action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action — only the introduction and referral.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill died without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The post-crisis rules stay in place, so the fund industry did not get the pricing flexibility it sought, and the run-risk protections remained for investors and taxpayers. Institutional investors who wanted stable-priced funds kept using alternatives.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Post-crisis fund safeguards stayed in place

for.name: Sen. Patrick Toomey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore stable-NAV money market fund options and ban direct bailouts of the funds.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or committee vote on the bill; it sat in the committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator sponsored the bill with two Democratic and one Republican cosponsor, but the Republican-chaired Banking Committee never acted on it, so no vote ever tested the split.

industries.note: The bill would have restored fixed $1 share pricing for all funds and waived default liquidity fees, freeing funds to market stable-priced products to large institutional investors. Its gain would come by unwinding post-crisis safeguards, shifting run risk onto investors and taxpayers; the direct-bailout ban is softened by an exception for broad-based emergency Fed programs.

Large cash managers — corporate treasurers, for example — preferred stable-priced funds before the reforms and lost access to them; the bill would have given that product back. Their interest runs alongside the investors who want the product, though the systemic risk is shared by everyone else.
